source_refs.note: Chapter 4 exercise (PDF 92-94), solved: 12 MCQs keyed with calculations (no key is printed), 10 short-answer, 2 descriptive and 4 numerical problems worked step by step. MCQ II, MCQ VI and Numerical Q.6 carry Book corrections.

blocks.text: Q.1 Four choices are given for each question. Select the correct choice.

blocks.prompt: I. Which one of the following statements is incorrect?

options.text: One mole of nitrogen gas contains Avogadro’s number of molecules
One mole of ozone gas contains Avogadro’s number of molecules
One mole of ozone contains Avogadro’s number of O atoms
One mole of hydrogen gas contains Avogadro’s number of molecules

blocks.explanation: One mole of O₃ contains 6.02 × 10²³ molecules; each molecule has 3 O atoms, so it contains 3 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.806 × 10²⁴ O atoms, not Avogadro's number. Statements (a), (b) and (d) are correct.

blocks.prompt: II. Which one of the following has maximum mass?
blocks.explanation:
m = n × M
N₂: 0.5 × 28.0 = 14.0 g
NH₃: 0.5 × 17.0 = 8.5 g
He: 0.5 × 4.0 = 2.0 g
CO: 0.5 × 28.0 = 14.0 g
N₂ and CO have the same, largest mass (14.0 g); see the Book correction below.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Two options are equally correct: N₂ and CO both have molar mass 28.0 g mol⁻¹, so 0.5 mol of each is 14.0 g. Option (a) is keyed; (d) is equally right. One of them should be changed (e.g. 0.5 mol of CO₂, 22.0 g, would make (d) the only answer).

blocks.prompt: III. Which one of the following gases will have maximum volume at STP?
blocks.explanation:
At STP volume depends only on moles (V = n × 22.4 dm³):
CO₂: 22/44 = 0.5 mol
N₂O: 88/44 = 2.0 mol → 44.8 dm³
CO: 28/28 = 1.0 mol
N₂: 28/28 = 1.0 mol
N₂O has the most moles, so the largest volume.

blocks.prompt: IV. Which of the following contains same number of atoms as present in 12 g of carbon?

options.text: 28 g of iron (Atomic mass of Fe = 56)
48 g of magnesium (Atomic mass of Mg = 24)
32 g of S₈ molecules (Atomic mass S = 32)
28 g of carbon monoxide (molar mass of CO = 28)

blocks.explanation:
12 g C = 1 mol of atoms.
Fe: 28/56 = 0.5 mol atoms
Mg: 48/24 = 2 mol atoms
S₈: 32 g of sulfur = 32/32 = 1 mol of S atoms (1/8 mol of S₈ molecules × 8)
CO: 28/28 = 1 mol of molecules = 2 mol of atoms
Only 32 g of S₈ has 1 mol (6.02 × 10²³) atoms.

blocks.prompt: V. Volume at S.T.P. of 22 g of CO₂ is same as that of:
blocks.explanation:
CO₂: 22/44 = 0.5 mol (11.2 dm³ at STP). Equal moles give equal volumes:
H₂: 2/2 = 1 mol
NH₃: 8.5/17 = 0.5 mol ✓
SO₂: 64/64 = 1 mol
CO: 7/28 = 0.25 mol

blocks.prompt: VI. 4.0 g of NaOH (molar mass 40 g mol⁻¹) contains same number of sodium ions as are present in:
blocks.explanation:
NaOH: 4.0/40 = 0.10 mol, so 0.10 mol Na⁺.
Na₂CO₃: 10.6/106 = 0.10 mol → 2 × 0.10 = 0.20 mol Na⁺
NaCl: 58.5/58.5 = 1.0 mol Na⁺
Na₂SO₄: 76/142 = 0.535 mol → 1.07 mol Na⁺
NaNO₃: 85/85 = 1.0 mol Na⁺
No option has exactly 0.10 mol Na⁺; (a), with 0.10 mol of Na₂CO₃, is the intended answer (see the Book correction).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: None of the printed options is exactly correct. 4.0 g NaOH has 0.10 mol Na⁺, but 10.6 g Na₂CO₃ has 0.20 mol Na⁺ (two Na⁺ per formula), 58.5 g NaCl and 85 g NaNO₃ have 1.0 mol and 76 g Na₂SO₄ has 1.07 mol. (a) is keyed as the intended answer (0.10 mol of Na₂CO₃, the closest). The same number of Na⁺ ions is in 5.3 g Na₂CO₃, 5.85 g NaCl, 7.1 g Na₂SO₄ or 8.5 g NaNO₃. Option (c) also prints “Na2SO4” without subscripts.

blocks.prompt: VII. A container holds 0.5 moles of an ideal gas at STP. What is the volume of the gas in dm³?
blocks.explanation: V = n × Vₘ = 0.5 mol × 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹ = 11.2 dm³

blocks.prompt: VIII. A solution contains 4.0 g of sodium hydroxide (NaOH, molar mass = 40.0 g mol⁻¹) in 250 cm³ of solution. What is the molar concentration of this solution?
IX. A solution contains 10.0 g of an unknown solute in 250 cm³ of solution. If the molar concentration of the solution is 0.20 mol dm⁻³, what is the molar mass of the solute?
blocks.explanation:
n = C × V = 0.20 mol dm⁻³ × 0.250 dm³ = 0.050 mol
M = m/n = 10.0 g / 0.050 mol = 200 g mol⁻¹

blocks.prompt: X. A sample of nitrogen gas (N₂, molar mass = 28.0 g mol⁻¹) has a mass of 14.0 g. How many nitrogen atoms are present in this sample?
blocks.explanation:
n(N₂) = 14.0 / 28.0 = 0.500 mol
molecules = 0.500 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.01 × 10²³
atoms = 2 × 3.01 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²³ (each N₂ has 2 atoms)

blocks.prompt: XI. A gas has a density of 1.43 g dm⁻³ at STP. What is the molar mass of the gas? (Molar volume at STP = 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹)
blocks.explanation: M = d × Vₘ = 1.43 g dm⁻³ × 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹ = 32.0 g mol⁻¹ (the gas could be O₂)

blocks.prompt: XII. A gas has a density of 1.96 g dm⁻³ at STP (0 °C and 1.00 atm). What is its molecular mass? (Molar volume at STP = 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹)
blocks.explanation: M = d × Vₘ = 1.96 g dm⁻³ × 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹ = 43.9 g mol⁻¹ ≈ 44.0 g mol⁻¹ (e.g. CO₂)

blocks.text: Q.2 Attempt the following short-answer questions:

blocks.prompt: a. How is the concept of mole derived from Avogadro’s number?
blocks.explanation: Avogadro's number (Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³) is the number of atoms in 12 g of carbon-12. The mole is defined as the amount of substance that contains this many entities (atoms, molecules, ions). So 1 mole = 6.02 × 10²³ particles, and its mass in grams is the molar mass; n = particles/Nₐ.

blocks.prompt:
b. Define the following terms with one example in each case.
(a) Molar mass (b) Molar volume (c) Molar concentration
blocks.explanation:
(a) Molar mass: the mass of one mole of a substance in grams (g mol⁻¹); e.g. CO₂ = 44.0 g mol⁻¹.
(b) Molar volume: the volume of one mole of an ideal gas at STP, 22.414 dm³ (≈ 22.4 dm³); e.g. 44.0 g CO₂ occupies 22.4 dm³.
(c) Molar concentration: moles of solute per dm³ of solution (C = n/V, mol dm⁻³); e.g. 27.64 g K₂CO₃ (0.2 mol) in 1 dm³ = 0.2 mol dm⁻³.

blocks.prompt: c. What do you mean by molar volume of a gas? How Avogadro’s number is related with molar volume?
blocks.explanation: Molar volume (Vₘ) is the volume of one mole of an ideal gas at STP (273.15 K, 1 atm): 22.414 dm³. By Avogadro's law equal volumes of gases at the same T and P have equal numbers of molecules, so 22.414 dm³ of any gas at STP contains Avogadro's number, 6.02 × 10²³, of molecules.

blocks.prompt: d. 39 g of potassium and 56 g of iron have equal number of atoms in them. Justify.
blocks.explanation:
n(K) = 39 g / 39 g mol⁻¹ = 1 mol
n(Fe) = 56 g / 56 g mol⁻¹ = 1 mol
One mole of any element has 6.02 × 10²³ atoms, so both have equal numbers of atoms; Fe atoms are heavier, so more mass is needed.

blocks.prompt: e. 4 g of He, 17 g of NH₃ and 64 g of SO₂ occupy separately the volumes of 22.414 dm³ although the sizes and masses of molecules of three gases are very different from each other.
blocks.explanation: Each is one mole: He 4/4, NH₃ 17/17, SO₂ 64/64 = 1 mol, i.e. 6.02 × 10²³ molecules. In a gas the molecules are very far apart, so the volume depends on the number of molecules, not on their size or mass (Avogadro's law). So each occupies 22.414 dm³ at STP.

blocks.prompt: f. Do you think that 1 mole of H₂ and 1 mole of NH₃ at 0 °C and 1 atm will have Avogadro’s number of particles?
blocks.explanation: Yes. One mole of any substance has 6.02 × 10²³ particles at any temperature and pressure: 6.02 × 10²³ H₂ molecules and 6.02 × 10²³ NH₃ molecules. At 0 °C and 1 atm (STP) each also occupies 22.4 dm³. (Atoms differ: 2Nₐ in H₂, 4Nₐ in NH₃.)

blocks.prompt: g. What is stoichiometry? Give the basic assumptions of stoichiometric calculations.
blocks.explanation:
Stoichiometry is the branch of chemistry that studies the quantitative relationship between reactants and products in a balanced chemical equation.
Assumptions: 1. All reactants are completely converted into products. 2. The law of conservation of mass and the law of definite proportions are obeyed. 3. No side reaction occurs.

blocks.prompt: h. What is a limiting reactant? How does it control the quantity of the product formed?
blocks.explanation: The limiting reactant is the reactant that is consumed first and so controls the amount of product. Once it is used up the reaction stops, so the maximum product depends only on its amount; the other reactant is left over (excess). E.g. 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O: with 2 mol H₂ and 2 mol O₂, H₂ is limiting and only 2 mol H₂O forms.

blocks.prompt: i. Differentiate theoretical and actual yields. How is the percentage yield of a reaction calculated?
blocks.explanation: % yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100; the greater the % yield, the more efficient the reaction.

rows: Amount of product calculated from the balanced equation
Amount of product actually obtained in the experiment
Usually less than the theoretical yield

blocks.prompt: j. What are the factors which are mostly responsible for the low yield of the products in chemical reactions?
blocks.explanation:
1. Losses in filtration, distillation, use of a separating funnel, washing, drying and crystallization when not done properly.
2. Some reactants take part in competing side reactions.
3. The reaction may be reversible; the backward reaction reduces the product.

blocks.prompt: Q. 3 Differentiate limiting and non-limiting reactants. How a limiting reactant is determined from a balanced chemical equation and given data?
blocks.explanation:
Reactants are often not taken in the ratio of the balanced equation; a cheap reactant is used in excess so that the costly one is fully converted, the product is maximum and the rate is higher.
Limiting reactant: consumed first; controls the maximum amount of product; the reaction stops when it is used up.
Non-limiting (excess) reactant: left unreacted after the reaction is complete.
Determining the limiting reactant (three steps):
1. Calculate the moles of each reactant from the given data (n = m/M, n = V/22.4 dm³ at STP, or n = C × V).
2. Using the mole ratio of the balanced equation, calculate the moles of product each reactant can give.
3. The reactant that gives the least product is the limiting reactant; the other is in excess.
Example (Sample Problem 4.19): CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, with 30 g CH₄ and 50 g O₂.
n(CH₄) = 30/16 = 1.875 mol → CO₂ = 1.875 mol
n(O₂) = 50/32 = 1.563 mol → CO₂ = 1.563/2 = 0.7815 mol
O₂ gives less CO₂, so O₂ is limiting; CO₂ = 0.7815 × 44 = 34.4 g. CH₄ used = 0.7815 mol, left = 1.875 − 0.7815 = 1.0935 mol = 17.5 g (excess).

rows: Does not control the amount of product
Gives the least amount of product in calculation
Gives more product in calculation than actually forms
Usually the cheap reactant, taken in excess

blocks.prompt: Q4. Differentiate actual and theoretical yields. Why the theoretical yield is always greater than actual yield?
blocks.explanation:
Theoretical yield: the maximum amount of product calculated from the balanced chemical equation for a given amount of the limiting reactant.
Actual yield: the amount of product actually obtained in the reaction.
% yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100; a higher % yield means a more efficient reaction.
Why the theoretical yield is greater:
1. Mechanical losses: product is lost during filtration, distillation, separation with a separating funnel, washing, drying and crystallization if not carried out properly.
2. Side reactions: some reactants take part in competing side reactions and form other products.
3. Reversible reactions: the backward reaction reduces the amount of product.
The calculation assumes complete conversion with no side reaction, which real reactions do not achieve, so the actual yield is less.
Example: from 3.00 g salicylic acid the theoretical yield of aspirin is 3.96 g; if 3.15 g is obtained, % yield = 3.15/3.96 × 100 = 79.5 % (Sample Problem 4.20, corrected).

rows: Assumes complete conversion, no side reaction
Affected by losses, side and reverse reactions
Fixed for a given amount of limiting reactant

blocks.prompt:
Q.5 A solution of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) is prepared by dissolving 2.00 g of solid sodium hydroxide in water to make a final volume of 250 cm³.
a) Calculate the number of moles of sodium hydroxide used.
b) Determine the molar mass of sodium hydroxide.
c) Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution in mol dm⁻³.
d) If more water is added to the above solution to raise the volume of solution to 500 cm³, what would be the concentration now?
blocks.explanation:
Given: m(NaOH) = 2.00 g, V₁ = 250 cm³ = 0.250 dm³, V₂ = 500 cm³ = 0.500 dm³ (Ar: Na 23.0, O 16.0, H 1.0)
b) Molar mass (needed first):
M(NaOH) = 23.0 + 16.0 + 1.0 = 40.0 g mol⁻¹
a) n = m/M
n = 2.00 g / 40.0 g mol⁻¹
n = 0.0500 mol
c) C = n/V
C = 0.0500 mol / 0.250 dm³
C = 0.200 mol dm⁻³
d) Dilution does not change the moles of NaOH:
C₂ = n/V₂ = 0.0500 mol / 0.500 dm³
C₂ = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ (doubling the volume halves the concentration; C₁V₁ = C₂V₂)

blocks.prompt:
Q.6 Ammonia gas (NH₃) reacts with oxygen gas (O₂) according to the following balanced equation:
4NH₃(g) + 5O₂(g) ⟶ 4NO(g) + 6H₂O(g)
In an experiment, 34.0 g of ammonia is reacted with 80.0 g of oxygen.
a) Determine the limiting reactant.
b) Calculate the maximum mass of nitrogen monoxide (NO) that can be formed.
c) Calculate the mass of the excess reactant remaining after the reaction is complete. (Relative atomic masses: H = 1.0, N = 14.0, O = 16.0)
blocks.explanation:
Given: m(NH₃) = 34.0 g, m(O₂) = 80.0 g; M(NH₃) = 14.0 + 3(1.0) = 17.0 g mol⁻¹, M(O₂) = 32.0 g mol⁻¹, M(NO) = 14.0 + 16.0 = 30.0 g mol⁻¹
Moles:
n(NH₃) = 34.0 / 17.0 = 2.00 mol
n(O₂) = 80.0 / 32.0 = 2.50 mol
a) NO from each reactant:
from NH₃: 4 mol NH₃ → 4 mol NO, so 2.00 mol NH₃ → 2.00 mol NO
from O₂: 5 mol O₂ → 4 mol NO, so 2.50 mol O₂ → (4/5) × 2.50 = 2.00 mol NO
Both give the same amount, 2.00 mol NO: the reactants are in the exact ratio 4 : 5 (2.00 : 2.50). Neither is in excess; both are used up completely (there is no single limiting reactant).
b) m(NO) = n × M = 2.00 mol × 30.0 g mol⁻¹ = 60.0 g
c) O₂ needed for 2.00 mol NH₃ = (5/4) × 2.00 = 2.50 mol = all the O₂ taken.
Excess reactant remaining = 0 g.
Check: 34.0 + 80.0 = 114.0 g = 60.0 g NO + 54.0 g H₂O (3.00 mol × 18.0).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The data make the reactants exactly stoichiometric: 34.0 g NH₃ (2.00 mol) and 80.0 g O₂ (2.50 mol) are in the 4 : 5 ratio of the equation. So there is no limiting or excess reactant, and part (c) gives 0 g. With, for example, 100 g of O₂ (3.13 mol), NH₃ would be limiting, NO would still be 60.0 g and 20.0 g of O₂ would remain.

blocks.prompt:
Q.7 When iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃) reacts with carbon monoxide (CO) in a blast furnace, iron metal (Fe) is produced according to the following equation:
Fe₂O₃(s) + 3CO(g) ⟶ 2Fe(s) + 3CO₂(g)
If 1.00 kg of iron(III) oxide is reacted with excess carbon monoxide, and 650 g of iron is obtained, what is the percentage yield of iron? (Aᵣ of O = 16.0, Fe = 55.8)
blocks.explanation:
Given: m(Fe₂O₃) = 1.00 kg = 1000 g, actual yield of Fe = 650 g; Aᵣ: Fe = 55.8, O = 16.0
M(Fe₂O₃) = 2(55.8) + 3(16.0) = 111.6 + 48.0 = 159.6 g mol⁻¹
n(Fe₂O₃) = 1000 g / 159.6 g mol⁻¹ = 6.266 mol
From the equation 1 mol Fe₂O₃ → 2 mol Fe:
n(Fe) = 2 × 6.266 = 12.53 mol
Theoretical yield of Fe = 12.53 mol × 55.8 g mol⁻¹ = 699 g
% yield = (actual / theoretical) × 100
% yield = (650 g / 699 g) × 100
% yield = 93.0 %

blocks.prompt: Q.8 PbSO₄ is precipitated when aqueous solutions of Na₂SO₄ and Pb(NO₃)₂ are mixed. Calculate the mass of PbSO₄ formed when 1.25 dm³ of 0.05 M Pb(NO₃)₂ and 2 dm³ of 0.025 M Na₂SO₄ are mixed.
blocks.explanation:
Given: Pb(NO₃)₂: C = 0.05 mol dm⁻³, V = 1.25 dm³; Na₂SO₄: C = 0.025 mol dm⁻³, V = 2 dm³; M(PbSO₄) = 303.3 g mol⁻¹
Na₂SO₄(aq) + Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) → PbSO₄(s) + 2NaNO₃(aq)
Net ionic: Pb²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → PbSO₄(s) (1 : 1)
n = C × V
n(Pb²⁺) = 0.05 × 1.25 = 0.0625 mol
n(SO₄²⁻) = 0.025 × 2 = 0.050 mol
SO₄²⁻ (0.050 mol) is less than Pb²⁺ (0.0625 mol), so SO₄²⁻ (Na₂SO₄) is the limiting reactant.
n(PbSO₄) = 0.050 mol
m(PbSO₄) = 0.050 mol × 303.3 g mol⁻¹ = 15.2 g
(Pb²⁺ left over: 0.0625 − 0.050 = 0.0125 mol.) This is the book's Sample Problem 4.18, whose answer, 15.2 g, agrees.
